output.summary: Current NIA-AA criteria classify Alzheimer's disease biologically by the AT(N) biomarker framework. Low CSF Aβ42 or a reduced Aβ42/40 ratio (A+), combined with elevated CSF p-tau181 or positive tau PET (T+), places an individual on the Alzheimer's continuum irrespective of clinical stage. Neurodegeneration markers (elevated total tau, FDG-PET hypometabolism, MRI hippocampal atrophy) provide additional staging information. AAN guidelines recommend neuropsychological testing as a cornerstone for characterizing MCI and tracking progression. Amyloid PET is appropriate for patients with unexplained progressive MCI when the etiology remains uncertain after standard clinical and MRI evaluation.

key_clinical_evidence: Word-finding difficulty as a presenting complaint in early AD is common and should not automatically redirect the workup toward primary progressive aphasia — the critical distinguishing feature is the relative severity of episodic memory impairment versus phonological and syntactic errors; neuropsychological testing is essential for this distinction

A mildly elevated TSH (6.2 mIU/L) with a normal Free T4 during a levothyroxine dose-adjustment period represents subclinical or undertreated hypothyroidism that deserves treatment optimization but does not adequately explain a 14-month progressive amnestic syndrome with MRI hippocampal atrophy — the two diagnoses are not mutually exclusive

The hallmark neuropsychological signature of amnestic AD is a disproportionate storage-type encoding deficit: severely impaired free recall with minimal improvement on cued recall or recognition — this pattern (HVLT-R delayed recall 2nd percentile with near-zero recognition discrimination index) is highly characteristic of hippocampal-predominant pathology

The AT(N) biomarker framework (NIA-AA 2018) classifies an individual as on the Alzheimer's continuum when A+ and T+ criteria are met regardless of clinical stage; A+T+N+ additionally confirms neurodegeneration, strengthening the biological diagnosis

APOE ε4 carrier status is a risk modifier that increases the likelihood of AD but is neither sufficient nor necessary for the diagnosis; it should not replace biomarker confirmation in clinical management
Cholinesterase inhibitors are the first-line symptomatic therapy for mild-to-moderate AD dementia; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Priya Venkataraman is a 67-year-old right-handed retired professor of comparative literature who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by her husband for evaluation of progressive word-finding difficulty and episodic memory lapses over the past 14 months. The patient herself initially attributed the word-finding trouble to 'retirement rust,' noting that she no longer gave lectures or engaged in academic writing, which she had done daily for 35 years. Her husband first became concerned approximately 14 months ago when he observed her pausing mid-sentence during dinner conversations, reaching for words she would previously have produced effortlessly. She has increasingly resorted to circumlocution and approximations during conversation. Over the past year, she has also begun repeating questions within the same sitting, sometimes asking the same question three to four times within an hour. Approximately eight months ago, the family noticed she was forgetting recent conversations entirely — her son would describe an event over the phone that she had no recall of by the following day. She has missed two scheduled doctor's appointments despite being reminded and has had increasing difficulty managing her calendar and correspondence, tasks she previously handled independently. She continues to drive to familiar locations, though her husband has noted she takes longer routes than necessary on two occasions. She was able to complete her grocery shopping with a list but requires the list, whereas previously she shopped from memory. Her book club participation has become strained; she reports losing the thread of novels she is reading and has had difficulty following plot discussions. Of note, her levothyroxine dose was increased from 75 mcg to 100 mcg approximately four months ago after a TSH of 6.2 mIU/L was found on routine labs; her primary care physician had attributed her subjective complaints partly to the borderline TSH at that time and deferred further workup pending thyroid optimization. Her husband reports no personality change, disinhibition, or apathy. She has no visual hallucinations, no gait difficulties, and no episodes of unexplained falls. She denies depressed mood, hopelessness, or anhedonia; she describes feeling frustrated and embarrassed about the word-finding difficulty but remains engaged and motivated. She has had no headaches, seizures, fever, weight loss, or focal neurological symptoms.
